title: Accelerators Create Matter from Energy
lead: Most of what is known about particle physics comes from accelerators, machines that give known particles enough energy to create new matter in collisions. This section describes the Van de Graaff and the cyclotron, the synchrotrons and linear accelerators that followed them, and the colliding beams that make more of the beam energy available for new particles.
objectives: State the principle of a cyclotron.
Explain the principle of a synchrotron.
Describe the voltage needed by an accelerator between accelerating tubes.
summary_html:
• A variety of particle accelerators have been used to explore the nature of subatomic particles and to test predictions of particle theories.
  • Modern accelerators used in particle physics are either large synchrotrons or linear accelerators.
  • The use of colliding beams makes much greater energy available for the creation of particles, and collisions between matter and antimatter allow a greater range of final products.
notes: The key to the AP item on the first hint that mass and energy conservation combine is carried as the book prints it, “(c), though this comes from Einstein's special relativity.”
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s own key. Three unkeyed problems are left out: the distance a W⁻ moves at 0.900c in 5.00 × 10⁻²⁵ s, the average gap voltage of SLAC’s 15,000 tubes, and the collision energy of 7.00-TeV protons and antiprotons at the LHC. The AP item on the kinetic energy a K⁻ needs to produce an Ω on a stationary proton is held for Particles, Patterns, and Conservation Laws, where Table 33.2 gives the masses it needs. Three AP items are unkeyed and carry AI-marked suggested approaches: the bowling balls and the tennis ball, the decay of a Z boson into kaons or electron-positron pairs, and the neutron’s decay. The four conceptual questions carry AI-marked suggested approaches. The module prints no Check Your Understanding box, so nothing is set inline.

figures.original_caption: Cyclotrons use a magnetic field to cause particles to move in circular orbits. As the particles pass between the plates of the Ds, the voltage across the gap is oscillated to accelerate them twice in each orbit.

(a) A synchrotron has a ring of magnets and accelerating tubes. The frequency of the accelerating voltages is increased to cause the beam particles to travel the same distance in shorter time. The magnetic field should also be increased to keep each beam burst traveling in a fixed-radius path. Limits on magnetic field strength require these machines to be very large in order to accelerate particles to very high energies. (b) A positive particle is shown in the gap between accelerating tubes. (c) While the particle passes through the tube, the potentials are reversed so that there is another acceleration at the next gap. The frequency of the reversals needs to be varied as the particle is accelerated to achieve successive accelerations in each gap.

This schematic shows the two rings of Fermilab’s accelerator and the scheme for colliding protons and antiprotons (not to scale). The Stanford Linear Accelerator was 3.2 km long and had the capability of colliding electron and positron beams. SLAC was also used to probe nucleons by scattering extremely short wavelength electrons from them. This produced the first convincing evidence of a quark structure inside nucleons in an experiment analogous to those performed by Rutherford long ago.

exercises.prompt: Which of the below was the first hint that conservation of mass and conservation of energy might need to be combined into one concept?

options: New particles showing up in accelerators.
answer.hint: Think of the first idea in which a particle’s mass had to be borrowed as energy for a short time.
answer.solution: (c), though this comes from Einstein's special relativity

exercises.prompt: How fast would two 7.0-kg bowling balls each have to be going in a collision to have enough spare energy to create a 0.10-kg tennis ball? (Ignore relativistic effects.) Can you explain why we don't see this in daily situations?

answer.solution: Let the balls meet head-on with equal speeds, so their total momentum is zero and all of their kinetic energy can go into new matter. The tennis ball needs $\kdE = \km\kc^{2}$ with $\km = 0.10\;\text{kg}$. Set the total kinetic energy of the two balls, $2 \times \frac{1}{2}Mv^{2} = Mv^{2}$ with $M = 7.0\;\text{kg}$, equal to that energy and solve for $v$; it comes out as a sizable fraction of the speed of light. Everyday collisions are many orders of magnitude slower, so the energy they have to spare is far too small to create even a tiny fraction of a gram of matter.

exercises.prompt: Using only energy-mass considerations, how many K<sup>0</sup> could a Z boson decay into? How many electrons and positrons could be produced this way?

answer.solution: Take the rest masses from Table 33.2 in Particles, Patterns, and Conservation Laws: the $Z^{0}$ at about $91\;\text{GeV}/c^{2}$, the $K^{0}$ at about $498\;\text{MeV}/c^{2}$ and the electron and positron at $0.511\;\text{MeV}/c^{2}$ each. Dividing the rest energy of the $Z^{0}$ by the rest energy of one $K^{0}$ and keeping the whole number gives the most kaons its energy could make. Electrons and positrons must be made in pairs to conserve charge, so divide the rest energy of the $Z^{0}$ by $2 \times 0.511\;\text{MeV}$ to find the number of pairs; there are as many electrons as positrons.

exercises.prompt: A π<sup>+</sup> and a π<sup>-</sup> are moving toward each other extremely slowly. When they collide, two π<sup>0</sup> are produced. How fast are they going? (Ignore relativistic effects.)

answer.hint: The charged pions have $139.6\;\text{MeV}/c^{2}$ each and the neutral ones $135.0\;\text{MeV}/c^{2}$; the rest energy left over is shared equally as the kinetic energy of the two $\pi^{0}$.

exercises.prompt: Assume that when a free neutron decays, it transforms into a proton and an electron. Calculate the kinetic energy of the electron.

answer.solution: The energy released is the rest energy the neutron has beyond the proton and the electron together, $\kdE = (m_{n} - m_{p} - m_{e})\kc^{2}$, with $939.6$, $938.3$ and $0.511\;\text{MeV}/c^{2}$ for the three masses. The proton is so much heavier than the electron that its recoil takes almost none of this, so the electron carries nearly all of it as kinetic energy. (In the real decay a neutrino is also made and shares the energy, which is why the electron’s energy is found to vary.)

exercises.prompt: The total energy in the beam of an accelerator is far greater than the energy of the individual beam particles. Why isn’t this total energy available to create a single extremely massive particle?

answer.solution: New particles are made in collisions between individual particles, one beam particle against one target particle or one particle of the other beam. Each collision can only convert the energy those two particles bring to it, $\kdE$, into mass $\km = \kdE/\kc^{2}$. The beam’s total energy is spread over an enormous number of separate particles that collide one pair at a time, so it is never brought together in one place at one moment to make a single particle.

exercises.prompt: Synchrotron radiation takes energy from an accelerator beam and is related to acceleration. Why would you expect the problem to be more severe for electron accelerators than proton accelerators?

answer.solution: At the same energy an electron, being about 2000 times less massive than a proton, moves much closer to the speed of light, and it needs much less force to bend it, so on the same ring it is given a far larger centripetal acceleration for each unit of mass. Radiation from an accelerated charge grows with its acceleration, so the electrons radiate away much more of their energy each turn. That is why the largest electron machines are linear accelerators, which do not bend the beam.

exercises.prompt: What two major limitations prevent us from building high-energy accelerators that are physically small?

answer.solution: First, the magnetic field needed to bend a particle in a circle grows with its momentum, and there is a limit to how strong a field even superconducting magnets can make, so a higher energy needs a larger radius. Second, a small ring bends the particles sharply, and the synchrotron radiation they give off grows with that acceleration, so a small machine loses too much energy each turn. A linear accelerator avoids bending, but it can only give the energy of the sum of its gap voltages, so it must be long.

exercises.prompt: What are the advantages of colliding-beam accelerators? What are the disadvantages?

answer.solution: Advantages: two beams meeting head-on have zero total momentum, so none of their energy must go into recoil and nearly all of it, twice the beam energy, is available to create new particles; a particle and its antiparticle can share one ring, circulating in opposite directions. Disadvantages: two beams are much more dilute than a solid target, so collisions are far rarer and each one is precious; the beams must be steered to meet very precisely at the detectors; and making, storing and accelerating antiparticles is difficult and costly.

exercises.prompt: At full energy, protons in the 2.00-km-diameter Fermilab synchrotron travel at nearly the speed of light, since their energy is about 1000 times their rest mass energy. (a) How long does it take for a proton to complete one trip around? (b) How many times per second will it pass through the target area?

parts.part: (a) the time for one trip around
parts.hint: Divide the circumference, $\pi$ times the diameter, by the speed of light.

parts.part: (b) the passes through the target area each second
parts.hint: The number of trips each second is one divided by the time for one trip.

exercises.prompt: What length track does a π+ traveling at 0.100 c leave in a bubble chamber if it is created there and lives for $2.60\times 10^{-8}\;\text{s}$? (Those moving faster or living longer may escape the detector before decaying.)

answer.hint: The track is the distance the pion covers in its lifetime, its speed times the time.

exercises.prompt: Because of energy loss due to synchrotron radiation in the LHC at CERN, only 5.00 MeV is added to the energy of each proton during each revolution around the main ring. How many revolutions are needed to produce 7.00-TeV (7000 GeV) protons, if they are injected with an initial energy of 8.00 GeV?

answer.hint: Divide the energy the protons must still gain, from 8.00 GeV to 7000 GeV, by the 5.00 MeV added each revolution.

exercises.prompt: When an electron and positron collide at the SLAC facility, they each have 50.0 GeV kinetic energies. What is the total collision energy available, taking into account the annihilation energy? Note that the annihilation energy is insignificant, because the electrons are highly relativistic.

answer.hint: Add the two kinetic energies and the rest energies of the electron and positron, $2 \times 0.511\;\text{MeV}$.
